title: A KING HAD HIS OWN SISTER AS HIS WIFE—AND THE BIBLE EVEN NAMES THEIR CHILDREN. BUT IS THAT REALLY WHAT SCRIPTURE SAYS?
paragraphs: A KING HAD HIS OWN SISTER AS HIS WIFE—AND THE BIBLE EVEN NAMES THEIR CHILDREN. BUT IS THAT REALLY WHAT SCRIPTURE SAYS?

One royal family. Several women named Tamar. A horrifying family scandal. And an ancient genealogy that exposes how easily a misunderstood Bible verse can become a convincing lie. What Scripture actually reveals is far more disturbing—and far more important—than the headline.
There are things in the Bible that make you stop reading.
Not because you doubt God.
But because you suddenly wonder whether you understood what you just read.
Imagine opening your Bible and encountering a claim that a powerful king married his own sister, fathered children with her, and had their names preserved in the sacred genealogies of Israel.
Your stomach turns.
You look at the references.
2 Samuel 13:1.
1 Chronicles 3:1–9.
And there they are. Real verses. Real names. A real royal family.
But something is wrong.
Because a Bible reference attached to a shocking statement does not automatically make that statement biblical truth.
And if you read these passages carefully, you will discover something even more unsettling than the original accusation.
The Bible does expose a royal household filled with sexual violence, betrayal, family dysfunction, and devastating consequences.
But it does not say that King David married his own sister.
Nor does it identify Tamar, David's daughter, as one of his wives.
That distinction matters.
Because sometimes the most dangerous distortion of Scripture is not a completely invented story.
It is a real biblical story with one crucial relationship changed.
And once that relationship changes, the entire meaning changes with it.
Stay with this, because the woman at the center of this confusion deserves something better than another sensational headline.
She deserves to have her story told truthfully.
And the Gospel has something to say about what happened to her.
The confusion begins in the royal household of King David.
David was Israel's celebrated warrior. The shepherd who defeated Goliath. The king who received God's covenant promise concerning his dynasty.
But behind the palace walls stood a family far more fractured than the songs of victory suggested.
First Chronicles 3:1–9 records the names of David's children and identifies several of their mothers.
Amnon was born to Ahinoam of Jezreel.
Daniel, called Chileab in 2 Samuel 3:3, was born to Abigail.
Absalom was born to Maacah, daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur.
Adonijah was born to Haggith.
Shephatiah was born to Abital.
Ithream was born to Eglah.
Later, the genealogy identifies children born to Bath-shua, generally understood to be Bathsheba, and mentions additional sons and concubines.
Then, almost unexpectedly, the Chronicler adds a name that changes the emotional weight of the entire record.
Tamar.
First Chronicles 3:9 reads in the King James Version:
"These were all the sons of David, beside the sons of the concubines, and Tamar their sister."
Read those final words again.
"Tamar their sister."
Not David's wife.
Not the mother of David's children.
Their sister.
The Hebrew is even more precise.
וְתָמָר אֲחוֹתָם
Ve-Tamar achotam.
Literally, "and Tamar, their sister."
The word אֲחוֹתָם (achotam) means "their sister."
It does not mean "his wife."
It does not describe a marriage.
It identifies a family relationship.
And that small distinction protects us from turning a woman's recorded identity into a claim the Bible never makes.
But why does the Chronicler specifically mention Tamar?
Why does her name stand out in a genealogy otherwise dominated by sons?
Scripture does not explicitly explain the Chronicler's reason.
What it does give us is another passage in which her name becomes inseparable from one of the most heartbreaking episodes in David's household.
And this is where the story becomes difficult.
Second Samuel 13:1 introduces Tamar as the beautiful sister of Absalom, David's son.
The Hebrew reads:
וּלְאַבְשָׁלוֹם בֶּן־דָּוִד אָחוֹת יָפָה וּשְׁמָהּ תָּמָר
Ule-Avshalom ben-David achot yafah, ush'mah Tamar.
The essential meaning is:
"Absalom the son of David had a beautiful sister, whose name was Tamar."
The verse then introduces Amnon, another son of David, who desired her.
Amnon and Tamar shared the same father but had different mothers.
They were half-siblings.
And what followed was not a romantic relationship, a legitimate marriage, or a biblical endorsement of forbidden intimacy.
It was abuse.

Amnon became consumed by his desire for Tamar. With the assistance of a cunning relative named Jonadab, he arranged circumstances that brought Tamar into his room under the appearance of caring for a sick family member.
She came to serve him.
She trusted the household enough to enter.
He used that access to trap her.
When his intentions became clear, Tamar resisted.
She pleaded with him not to violate her.
She appealed to the moral standards of Israel.
She warned him about the disgrace and devastation his actions would cause.
But he refused to listen.
Second Samuel 13:14 states:
"Howbeit he would not hearken unto her voice: but, being stronger than she, forced her, and lay with her."
There is no ambiguity about the central act.
Tamar was raped.
The Bible does not describe her as consenting.
It does not present Amnon's behavior as a legitimate expression of love.
It records his refusal to hear her and his use of superior physical strength.
And then comes one of the cruelest turns in the narrative.
After violating Tamar, Amnon rejected her.
The man who claimed to be overwhelmed by love suddenly treated her with hatred.
Second Samuel 13:15 says that his hatred afterward was greater than the love he had claimed before.
That single verse exposes a terrible truth about sinful desire.
What Amnon called love was never the self-giving love Scripture commands.
It was possession.
It was appetite.
It was power without righteousness.
And when he had taken what he wanted, he discarded the person whose dignity he had violated.
Perhaps someone reading this knows what it feels like to be trusted only until another person gets what they want.
Perhaps someone understands the devastation of being betrayed by a person who should have been safe.
Perhaps the wound was never physical violence, but manipulation, abandonment, exploitation, or betrayal.
The details may be different.
The pain of having your humanity disregarded can remain for years.
And here is something you need to hear clearly.
What happened to Tamar was Amnon's sin. It was not Tamar's moral failure.
Her resistance mattered.
Her voice mattered.
Her dignity mattered.
And her suffering mattered enough that Scripture did not erase it from the royal record.
After the assault, Tamar tore the special garment she wore as a virgin daughter of the king, placed ashes upon her head, and went away crying.
Second Samuel 13:19 describes her public grief.
She did not emerge from that room as the guilty party.
She emerged as someone grievously wronged.
Then Absalom, her brother, took her into his household.
Second Samuel 13:20 says that Tamar remained desolate in Absalom's house.
The Hebrew word used there is שֹׁמֵמָה (shomemah), conveying a condition of devastation or desolation.
Scripture does not tell us everything about Tamar's later life.
It does not give us a detailed account of her healing.
It does not record her marriage, her death, or the full course of her future.
We should not invent a happy ending that the biblical author never supplied.
But neither should we mistake the Bible's silence about her later years for God's indifference to her suffering.
There is another detail that should trouble every reader.
When King David heard what Amnon had done, he became very angry.
Second Samuel 13:21 records his anger.
Yet the narrative does not describe David administering justice to Amnon.
Anger appears.
Justice is not shown.
And in that unresolved space, Absalom's bitterness grew.
Two years later, Absalom arranged Amnon's murder.
The family descended further into vengeance, estrangement, rebellion, and bloodshed.
What began as one man's sinful violation became part of a widening catastrophe inside the royal house.
This does not make Absalom's murder righteous.
It does show how grievous wrongdoing, when left without proper justice and repentance, can become part of a destructive chain of further sins.
Now return to the original claim.
"A king had his own sister as his wife—and the Bible names their children."
Where, exactly, does the Bible say that?
Not in 2 Samuel 13:1.
Not in 1 Chronicles 3:1–9.
Those passages describe David's children, their mothers, and Tamar's identity as a sister within the family.
They do not record David marrying Tamar.
They do not identify children born from such a marriage.
And they certainly do not authorize us to convert the story of Amnon's assault into an ordinary royal marriage.
There is, however, another genealogical detail worth examining.
Second Samuel 14:27 says that Absalom had three sons and a daughter named Tamar, who was a beautiful woman.
That means the biblical narrative also records a daughter of Absalom named Tamar.
So we encounter Tamar, the daughter of David and sister of Absalom, and another Tamar, the daughter of Absalom.
The repetition of a name within a family is not evidence that the two women were the same person.
Nor is it evidence of an incestuous marriage.
Ancient biblical genealogies frequently repeat names across generations.
The name Tamar itself, תָּמָר (Tamar), means "palm tree."
It is also the name of the woman whose story appears in Genesis 38, an entirely different episode involving Judah and his family.
That account has its own complicated moral and historical context.
It must not be confused with the Tamar of 2 Samuel 13.
Different people.
Different generations.
Different relationships.
Different narratives.
This is why biblical genealogies must be read with care.
A name appearing twice does not prove a person appears twice.
A woman appearing near the names of a king's children does not make her his wife.
And a verse containing a disturbing family event does not mean God approves of the event it records.
Description is not endorsement.
This is especially important when studying ancient royal households.
The Bible does record marriages between close relatives in certain historical settings.
Abraham described Sarah as his half-sister in Genesis 20:12.
That passage deserves to be read on its own terms.
The Bible also records the later prohibition against sexual relations between siblings in Leviticus 18:9 and 18:11, and the corresponding condemnation in Leviticus 20:17.
Those laws are not interchangeable with every earlier historical narrative, and they should not be used to erase the chronological and covenantal contexts of the texts.
Yet neither should the existence of an ancient account be treated as moral permission for the behavior it describes.
Scripture records many things that Scripture also condemns.
Polygamy.
Deception.
Violence.
Adultery.
Murder.
Exploitation.
The Bible is remarkably unflinching about the failures of its most prominent human figures.
And that brings us to David himself.
David was not a flawless hero.
He was a king who committed adultery with Bathsheba and arranged the death of her husband, Uriah.
Second Samuel 11 tells that story.
Second Samuel 12 records the prophet Nathan confronting David.
David's royal position did not make his wrongdoing righteous.
His covenant calling did not exempt him from accountability.
And his repentance did not magically erase every earthly consequence of his actions.
This matters because Christians sometimes feel pressured to defend every action of a biblical figure whom God used.
But faithfulness to Scripture requires the opposite.
We must allow the Bible to expose sin wherever it appears.
Even in a palace.
Even in a family admired by an entire nation.
Even in the life of a king whose psalms still comfort believers today.
The Bible does not need us to sanitize David.
It needs us to read his story truthfully.
And then, beyond David's failures, to see the greater King to whom God's redemptive promises ultimately point.
Jesus Christ.
Think about the contrast.
Amnon used his power to take from someone vulnerable.
Jesus, though truly Lord, humbled Himself and gave Himself for others.
Amnon refused to hear Tamar's pleading.
Jesus welcomed the afflicted, the rejected, and the brokenhearted.
Amnon's supposed love turned into hatred when his selfish desire was satisfied.
Christ's love was demonstrated in sacrificial obedience, even unto death.
Philippians 2:8 declares that Jesus "humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross."
The difference is not merely between a bad man and a good man.
It is between sinful humanity, corrupted by self-serving desire, and the sinless Savior who came to redeem sinners.
The Gospel does not teach that every person who has suffered will receive complete earthly restoration immediately.
It does not promise that all traumatic memories disappear when someone prays.
And it never requires a victim to deny wrongdoing, abandon appropriate boundaries, or refuse legitimate justice in order to prove forgiveness.
But it does announce that evil does not have the final word.
Psalm 34:18 says:
"The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit."
That promise does not trivialize suffering.
It reveals the character of the God who draws near to those in distress.
And Isaiah 61:1 speaks of good news to the meek and the binding up of the brokenhearted—words Jesus reads in connection with His mission in Luke 4:18–21.
The Christ revealed in the Gospels is not indifferent to the wounded.
He sees people whom others overlook.
He restores dignity to those treated as disposable.
He confronts hypocrisy.
He calls sinners to repentance.
And through His death and resurrection, He opens the way to forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life.
But there is another side of this message that we must not avoid.
Some readers will recognize themselves in Tamar's suffering.
Others may recognize something of Amnon's selfishness.
Not necessarily the same crime, but the same terrible temptation to place personal desire above another person's dignity.
To manipulate.
To exploit.
To excuse.
To refuse correction.
To call something love when it is actually control.
The Gospel does not invite us to disguise these sins with religious language.
It calls us to bring them into the light.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
That is not permission to continue harming others.
True repentance turns away from sin, accepts accountability, and seeks to make wrongs right wherever possible.
Grace is not a hiding place for unrepentant cruelty.
Grace is God's undeserved mercy in Christ, calling sinners out of darkness and into transformed living.
And for the person who has been wounded by someone else's sin, there is another truth.
You do not have to accept responsibility for what another person chose to do to you.
You are not required to call evil good.
You are not obligated to pretend that a wound has healed when it has not.
Christ-centered healing can include prayer, wise pastoral care, trustworthy community, professional counseling, protection, and the pursuit of justice.
Seeking help is not a betrayal of faith.
And you are not less loved by God because your recovery takes time.
Now consider something remarkable about the genealogy of Jesus.
Matthew 1:6 does not conceal David's failure.
It identifies Solomon's mother by reference to Uriah, the husband David had wronged.
The genealogy itself carries a reminder of royal sin.
And yet that same genealogy leads us toward Jesus Christ.
This is not a declaration that sin was harmless.
It is a testimony that God's redemptive purpose was not defeated by human wickedness.
David's house was marked by scandal.
Yet God remained faithful to His promise.
Jesus, the Son of David, came not to imitate David's failures but to fulfill God's saving purpose.
He is the righteous King.
The Savior without sin.
The One who gave His life as a ransom for many, as Mark 10:45 declares.
And here, at last, the deeper meaning of this story begins to emerge.
The Bible does not preserve these scandals so we can enjoy the humiliation of broken people. It preserves truth that warns us about sin and directs us toward our need for redemption.
We must never turn Tamar's suffering into entertainment.
We must never use her story merely to create outrage.
And we must never invent a marriage or children that Scripture does not record simply because a sensational claim attracts attention.
If we truly love God's Word, truth must matter more than virality.
If we truly love people, their dignity must matter more than engagement.
And if we truly follow Jesus, we must care about the wounded as well as the wayward.
Maybe that is the most important question this passage leaves with us.
Not merely, "Did a king marry his own sister?"
The cited passages do not support that claim.
But rather:
What happens when people have power without righteousness?
What happens when families protect reputations while wounded members suffer?
What happens when anger replaces justice?
What happens when desire is mistaken for love?
And what happens when people who know the language of faith forget the character of the God they claim to serve?
Those questions are not confined to ancient Jerusalem.
They belong in our homes.
Our churches.
Our relationships.
Our private conversations.
And our own hearts.
Perhaps you began reading because the headline shocked you.
Perhaps you stayed because the story disturbed you.
But I pray you leave remembering something far greater than a royal scandal.
Jesus Christ is not another powerful man who came to take what He wanted. He is the righteous King who came to give His life for sinners.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that human beings are innocent.
Not that the world is fair.
Not that every wound is quickly healed.
But that the holy Son of God entered our fallen world, bore our sins upon the cross, rose victorious from the grave, and now calls us to repentance and faith.
He offers forgiveness to the repentant.
He gives hope to the wounded.
He brings sinners into new life.
And He promises a coming kingdom in which evil and death will not reign forever.
Revelation 21:4 looks toward the day when God will wipe away every tear and death, sorrow, crying, and pain will be no more.
Tamar's story reminds us how deeply this world needs such a King.
And Jesus is that King.
So before you leave this article, consider what God may be confronting in your heart.
Have you been carrying a wound that you have never felt safe enough to acknowledge?
Have you been defending a sin that you know needs to be confessed?
Have you been treating Scripture as a collection of shocking stories instead of the Word that reveals the holy and merciful God?
Or have you been wondering whether the broken chapters of your life have made redemption impossible?
They have not placed you beyond the reach of Christ.
Come to Him.
Not with a manufactured testimony.
Not with religious performance.
Not with the illusion that you have everything together.
Come with the truth.
Because Jesus does not require us to invent a spotless past before we can receive His mercy.
He calls us to repent, believe, and follow Him.
And if this story touched something personal, I want to invite you into a conversation that is deeper than a passing reaction.
You do not need to disclose painful personal details publicly. A few honest words are enough.
Someone in your family may need this message.
A friend may be quietly questioning God's goodness because of something terrible that happened to them.
Another believer may be struggling with the difference between forgiveness and excusing evil.
And someone who has never opened a Bible may need to discover that Christianity does not require pretending its human heroes were perfect.
Not merely to spread a dramatic headline, but to spread the truth that stands behind it.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, spiritually complacent Christians, seekers, and even those who do not yet believe to follow along.
Not everyone who encounters a biblical article will immediately agree.
But everyone deserves an opportunity to encounter the Gospel faithfully presented.
There is a difference between reading one article and helping make it possible for many more people to encounter sound biblical teaching.
Every article takes study, care, time, and a commitment to presenting Scripture faithfully.
Our desire is to continue producing resources that do more than stir emotions for a moment.
We want to help people open their Bibles, understand the Gospel, confront sin, grow in grace, and walk faithfully with Jesus Christ.
Think of it as a voluntary ministry offering—an expression of generosity toward a Gospel-centered mission you believe is worth supporting.
Scripture teaches believers to give willingly, not under pressure.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
Your faithful sharing may place a message of biblical hope before someone we could never reach on our own.
The reason is Jesus Himself.
Our hope is that these resources help you move beyond a moment of inspiration into a life of Scripture, prayer, repentance, obedience, and spiritual maturity.
Not to make a spectacle of ancient scandals.
Not to turn human suffering into religious entertainment.
Not to elevate any earthly king.
But to proclaim the Savior who stands above every failed king and every broken kingdom.
The genealogy records Tamar's name.
The narrative records her suffering.
The Bible refuses to pretend the royal family was righteous merely because it was royal.
And the Gospel directs our eyes beyond that broken household to the One who is perfectly righteous.
The world may remember the scandal that wounded a family, but the Gospel proclaims the King whose grace can redeem sinners and whose coming kingdom will finally make all things new.
